0.title: Covenant Love and the Gospel
0.overview:
Marriage is not a human invention that God later blessed — it is a divine institution that God established before humanity had a chance to propose alternatives. In the garden, before the Fall, before sin, before any shadow of disorder, God said: "It is not good for the man to be alone" (Gen 2:18) — and he made a woman and brought her to the man. The first wedding was officiated by God himself.

But the Bible's theology of marriage is richer and stranger than even this beginning suggests. Marriage, Paul tells us in Ephesians 5, is a mystery — a word he uses for truths hidden in God until their appointed time of revelation. The mystery is this: marriage, from the very beginning, was designed to be a living drama of the gospel, a sign pointing to the relationship between Christ and his church. Every Christian marriage is, whether the couple knows it or not, a public sermon about the love of Christ for his people.

This is simultaneously the most exalting and the most demanding thing that can be said about marriage. Exalting, because it means that ordinary Christian marriages — with all their imperfections and dailiness — are participating in something cosmic. Demanding, because it means that the standard of a Christian marriage is not societal convention or personal happiness but the self-giving, covenant-keeping love of Christ for his church.

Six units: (1) The Foundation — marriage as creation ordinance and gospel sign; (2) Covenant — what makes a marriage a marriage; (3) Husbands — the call to Christlike servant leadership; (4) Wives — the call to gospel-shaped strength; (5) When Marriage Is Hard — conflict, forgiveness, and the long road; (6) Marriage, Singleness, and the Kingdom — both callings honoured.

1.title: The Foundation: Marriage as Creation Ordinance and Gospel Sign
1.overview:
Marriage is a creation ordinance — an institution established by God in creation, before the Fall, intended for all humanity and not merely for the people of God. This means that marriage has a design, a purpose, and a structure written into creation itself, not merely into the Mosaic law or the church's tradition. When Jesus was asked about divorce, he went back to the beginning (Matt 19:4–6) — back past Moses, past Sinai, to creation. The structure of marriage is not negotiable because it is not a human construction.

Genesis 2:24 gives the blueprint: a man leaves his father and mother and holds fast to his wife, and they become one flesh. Three elements: leaving (the severance of the prior primary bond), holding fast (the establishment of a new, permanent covenant bond), and one flesh (the physical, emotional, and spiritual union that the covenant creates). This three-part structure is not merely ancient Near Eastern custom — Jesus and Paul both cite it as the normative pattern for all time (Matt 19:5, Eph 5:31).

And then Paul's astonishing parenthesis in Ephesians 5:32 — "This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church." The one-flesh union of husband and wife is a sign — not a symbol in the weak modern sense but a sign in the biblical sense: a real, enacted representation of a deeper reality. The marriage covenant points to and participates in the covenant between Christ and his people. This does not make marriage merely instrumental (as though its only purpose is to teach a lesson) — it makes it glorious, because the reality it signifies is the most glorious reality in the universe.
1.theology:
The purposes of marriage: The Reformation tradition identified three purposes of marriage: the procreation and nurture of children (Gen 1:28); the mutual companionship and help of husband and wife (Gen 2:18); and the remedy for sexual immorality (1 Cor 7:2–5). The contemporary evangelical tradition has rightly emphasised companionship — the profound friendship between husband and wife — as central. Tim Keller adds a fourth purpose drawn from Ephesians 5: marriage as a means of mutual sanctification, in which each spouse is an instrument of the other's growth into Christlikeness.

Marriage as covenant: Malachi 2:14 calls marriage a covenant — not a contract (which is a legal arrangement of mutual obligations that can be dissolved when obligations are not met) but a covenant (which is a binding, solemn, self-giving promise that creates a relationship). The difference is crucial: in a contract, I give what I agreed to give and expect what was promised in return; in a covenant, I give myself and commit to the relationship regardless of what I receive. Marriage is a covenant because the God who instituted it is a covenant God — and the love it calls for is the love that keeps promises regardless of cost.

The gospel and marriage: Ephesians 5:25–33 does not merely compare marriage to the gospel — it grounds the husband-wife relationship in the Christ-church relationship. The husband's love for his wife is not merely inspired by Christ's love for the church; it is to be patterned after it, powered by it, and accountable to it. The wife's response to her husband is not merely analogous to the church's response to Christ; it is an enacted participation in that response. Every Christian marriage is a living exegesis of the gospel.
1.examples:
Keller on marriage as a mirror: Tim Keller, in The Meaning of Marriage, argues that marriage is designed to hold up a mirror to each partner — showing them what they actually are, not what they imagine themselves to be. The intimacy of marriage strips away pretension and reveals the real self. This is not a design flaw — it is the design. Marriage is a crucible of sanctification: the closest human relationship is the one in which our idols, our fears, our selfishness, and our need for grace are most fully exposed. The couple who understands this does not run from the hard seasons of marriage but stays in them, trusting that God is using the crucible.

Augustine on the three goods: Augustine identified the three goods of marriage as proles (children), fides (faithfulness), and sacramentum (the sacred bond — its indissolubility as a sign of the covenant). These three goods have shaped the church's theology of marriage for fifteen centuries. The modern crisis of marriage — soaring divorce rates, declining marriage rates, confusion about its purpose — is in large part a crisis of having abandoned Augustine's framework without replacing it with anything of comparable theological depth.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus calls this verse the foundation of the theology of marriage (Matt 19:5), and it repays slow reading. Leave — a decisive, permanent transfer of primary loyalty. The leaving is not geographical (you may live next door to your parents) but relational: the marriage relationship now takes priority over the family of origin. Hold fast — the Hebrew word (dabaq) is used for cleaving to God (Deut 10:20), for Ruth's loyalty to Naomi (Ruth 1:14). It is the language of covenant faithfulness, determined and tenacious. One flesh — not merely physical union but the comprehensive joining of two lives into one. The three elements together describe a covenant so total and so binding that Jesus says what God has joined, let no one separate.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh." This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul quotes Genesis 2:24 and then reveals what the Spirit encoded in it from the beginning: the one-flesh union of husband and wife is a mystery — a hidden truth now revealed — pointing to the union of Christ and his church. The marriage covenant was always a gospel sign, even before the gospel was explicitly announced. Every wedding in history has been, whether the couple knew it or not, a re-enactment of the story of the divine Bridegroom and his Bride. The Christian couple who understands this carries a weight and a glory into their marriage that mere romantic partnership cannot provide.

verseByVerse.quote: ...the LORD was witness between you and the wife of your youth, to whom you have been faithless, though she is your companion and your wife by covenant. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The prophet confronts Israel's casual divorce with a bracing reminder: the LORD was witness at your wedding. God was present, God heard the vows, God holds the covenant. This is why marriage is not dissoluble by mutual preference — it is a covenant made before God, and covenant obligations do not dissolve because one party finds them inconvenient. The phrase wife of your youth — the one who shared your beginning, who has walked the long road with you — is tender as well as binding. The man who was faithless to this covenant was not merely behaving poorly; he was betraying a partner in a God-witnessed covenant.

verseByVerse.quote: So they are no longer two but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus grounds the permanence of marriage in the act of God — not in the sentiment of the couple, not in the approval of the state, not in the continuation of romantic feelings, but in the creative act of God who joins what was two into one. The joining is God's act; the separating is man's act; and what man proposes to do, Jesus forbids. This is not legalism — it is the protection of the most intimate human relationship from the casual casualness of a culture that treats marriage as a renewable contract. The permanence of marriage is the security within which the intimacy of one flesh can fully develop.

2.title: Covenant: What Makes a Marriage a Marriage
2.overview:
The word that defines marriage in Scripture is not love — though love is essential. It is not compatibility — though friendship is foundational. The word is covenant. A covenant is a solemn, binding, self-giving promise made before God that creates a relationship. In the biblical world, covenants were ratified with blood — an acted declaration that said: may this happen to me if I break this promise. The wedding vow is a covenant oath: a self-binding promise made before God and witnesses that creates a new reality and obligates the person who makes it regardless of future feelings or circumstances.

The contrast with the contemporary understanding of marriage could not be sharper. Modern Western culture has largely reduced marriage to an elevated romantic partnership — a contractual arrangement that continues as long as both parties find it fulfilling and dissolves when they do not. The decisive test is subjective: "Are we still happy? Are we still in love? Are we still fulfilled?" The biblical test is objective: "Did we make a covenant? Did God witness it? Have we kept it?"

This does not mean that feelings are unimportant or that unhappy marriages are acceptable — the biblical call is for deep love, genuine friendship, and abiding joy in the marriage relationship. But it does mean that the feelings are not the foundation. The covenant is the foundation on which the feelings are built, protected, and sustained. The couple who treats their marriage as a covenant — who keeps their promises even when the feelings are cold, who does the work of love even when love is not feeling easy — is the couple whose feelings have the best chance of being genuinely warm over the long haul.
2.theology:
Covenant vs. contract: Michael Horton's analysis of the covenant concept is illuminating here. A contract is a legal exchange of goods and services between parties who remain essentially self-interested — it exists for mutual benefit, and when the benefit ceases, the contract can be dissolved. A covenant creates a relationship, a bond between persons, that has moral weight independent of mutual benefit. The covenant of marriage creates a "we" that is more than the sum of the two "I's" — and that "we" has moral claims on both parties regardless of how either feels on any given day.

The vow as speech act: The wedding vow is a performative speech act — it does not merely describe a reality, it creates one. When the couple says "I will," something happens: a marriage comes into existence that did not exist a moment before. This means that the marriage is not made by the feelings (which may come and go) but by the word (which, once spoken before God, stands). The couple who said "I will" in health and sickness, wealth and poverty, better and worse — those words are still in force. That is both the burden and the beauty of the covenant.

Covenant faithfulness as love: The Hebrew word hesed — God's covenant love, his steadfast loving-kindness — is the model for covenant faithfulness in marriage. Hesed is not a feeling; it is a commitment. It is the love that keeps showing up regardless of how the other person responds. It is the love that Ruth showed Naomi: "Where you go I will go" (Ruth 1:16) — not conditional on Naomi's being attractive or easy to love, but committed because the bond is real and the promise stands. This is the love that Christian marriage is called to embody.
2.examples:
Robertson McQuilkin and covenant faithfulness: Robertson McQuilkin was president of Columbia Bible College when his wife Muriel began to show symptoms of Alzheimer's. As her condition worsened, he resigned his prestigious post to care for her full-time. His reason, in his own words: "She sacrificed for me for thirty years. It's now my turn." But more deeply: he had made a covenant. "In sickness and in health" was not a formula he had recited — it was a promise he had made to a person, before God, and he intended to keep it. McQuilkin's decision moved thousands of people precisely because it made visible what covenant love actually looks like.

Hosea's marriage as covenant theology: God commanded Hosea to marry Gomer, who proved unfaithful — and then commanded him to take her back after her infidelity (Hos 3:1). The command was the enactment of God's own relationship with Israel: a covenant people who had gone after other gods, and a covenant God who came after them anyway. Hosea's marriage was a living parable of divine hesed — covenant love that pursues the faithless, pays the price of redemption, and restores the broken relationship. Every Christian marriage is called to this pattern, in its own degree: pursuing, forgiving, restoring, because we have been pursued, forgiven, and restored.

verseByVerse.quote: But Ruth said, "Do not urge me to leave you or to return from following you. For where you go I will go, and where you lodge I will lodge. Your people shall be my people, and your God my God. Where you die I will die, and there will I be buried." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This covenant declaration — made between a daughter-in-law and her mother-in-law, not between husband and wife — is nonetheless the most beautiful portrait of covenant faithfulness in all of Scripture. Ruth commits herself completely: place, people, God, and even burial ground. Nothing is held back; no exit clause is reserved. This is what covenant love looks like in practice: it burns the boats, it closes the escape routes, it says "I am yours and that is final." Many wedding ceremonies read these words, and rightly so — they describe not the romantic feeling of falling in love but the covenantal act of choosing love regardless of what comes.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to me, "Go again, love a woman who is loved by another man and is an adulteress, even as the LORD loves the children of Israel, though they turn to other gods and love cakes of raisins." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God's command to Hosea is the most demanding thing ever commanded of a spouse: go back and love the one who betrayed you, because that is what I do with my faithless people. This is not romanticising infidelity or minimising its devastation — it is revealing the nature of divine covenant love, which pursues the faithless at cost to itself. The marriage that has survived betrayal and returned to covenant faithfulness is not a lesser marriage — it is, in some ways, a deeper enactment of the gospel than the marriage that has never been tested. The couple who knows what forgiveness costs because they have paid it has understood something about the cross that comfortable couples have not yet learned.

verseByVerse.quote: Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm, for love is strong as death, jealousy is fierce as the grave. Its flashes are flashes of fire, the very flame of the LORD. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The Song of Solomon celebrates the passionate, physical, exclusive love of husband and wife with a directness that makes careful readers blush. The seal upon the heart, the seal upon the arm — both public and private, both felt and displayed. The comparison to death is not morbid but emphatic: death is relentless, unstoppable, tenacious. So is covenant love. It does not release its hold; it does not tire; it does not look for an exit. The phrase the very flame of the LORD — translated some as "a most vehement flame" or "a flame of Yah" — hints that the passion of covenant love is not merely human but is, in some mysterious way, a participation in the burning love of God himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Love bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's hymn to love is not romantic poetry — it is a demanding description of covenant faithfulness. Bears all things: the word is stego — to cover, to roof over, to protect. Covenant love covers the other's failures rather than exposing them (Prov 10:12). Believes all things: generous interpretation, assuming the best rather than the worst. Hopes all things: the covenant love that does not give up on the other person's capacity for growth and change. Endures all things: hupomenei — remains under pressure rather than escaping it. These four verbs describe a love that is active, costly, patient, and indestructible — not because the person possessing it is exceptionally strong but because the God who commands it supplies it.

3.title: Husbands: The Call to Christlike Servant Leadership
3.overview:
Ephesians 5:25 is the most demanding verse ever addressed to a husband: "Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her." The standard is not romantic affection, not mutual kindness, not even sacrificial commitment in the general sense. The standard is the cross. The love that is required of husbands is the love that went to Calvary — the love that absorbed the full weight of the other's need, that gave everything without reservation, that served the beloved's flourishing at infinite cost to itself.

This places the husband's calling in a radically different light from both the authoritarian model (the husband as overlord, commanding submission and receiving service) and the egalitarian model (the husband and wife as interchangeable partners with no differentiated responsibilities). The New Testament call is for headship — real, genuine, responsible leadership — but a headship defined entirely by the pattern of the Servant-King who washed feet and died on a cross. Authority exercised as Christ exercised his authority always looks, to the onlooker, less like power and more like sacrifice.

The Greek word for love in Ephesians 5:25 is agape — the love that chooses the other's good regardless of what it costs the self. This is not the love that the husband feels when he is attracted to his wife; it is the love he exercises when the feelings are absent, when the relationship is hard, when the cost is high. It is a commanded love — a love that the husband is required to show regardless of how he feels, because it is rooted not in emotion but in covenant commitment and Christlike character.
3.theology:
Headship and servant leadership: The husband's headship (Eph 5:23) is explicitly patterned on Christ's headship of the church — and Christ's headship is servant headship (Mark 10:45). The head who died for the body he leads is not a hierarchy of command but a hierarchy of sacrifice. The husband who leads his marriage by asking "What can I give?" rather than "What can I get?" or "What am I owed?" is exercising headship as Ephesians intends it. Wayne Grudem and others in the complementarian tradition have insisted that headship is not oppression but responsibility — the husband answers before God for the leadership of the home.

Sanctifying love: Ephesians 5:26–27 describes what Christ's love for the church aims at: washing her, sanctifying her, presenting her to himself in splendour. The husband's love for his wife has the same goal: not his own comfort or status but her flourishing — her spiritual, emotional, physical, and relational growth. The husband who prays for his wife, who encourages her gifts, who creates the conditions for her to flourish, who speaks words that build rather than diminish — this husband is loving as Ephesians commands. The test is not "Does she serve me?" but "Am I serving her?"

Understanding and honour: 1 Peter 3:7 adds two more dimensions to the husband's calling: he is to live with his wife "according to knowledge" (understanding her, knowing her, attending to who she actually is rather than who he imagines her to be) and to show her honour as a fellow heir of the grace of life. The respect commanded here is not merely courteous — it is the honour due to a co-heir of grace, an equal in dignity before God, whose prayers alongside her husband rise to the same Father.
3.examples:
C.S. Lewis on charity in marriage: Lewis, in The Four Loves, observes that the presence of eros (romantic love) in marriage does not guarantee the presence of charity (agape). Eros can be intensely self-focused — desiring the beloved primarily for the feelings they produce in the lover. Charity is other-focused — choosing the beloved's good. A marriage that begins with eros but never develops charity will eventually run dry, because eros fluctuates with circumstances and age. The marriage that adds charity to eros — that chooses the other's good as a matter of principle and practice — has a foundation that withstands the fluctuations.

The husband as gardener: John Piper uses the image of the gardener to describe the husband's calling: he is to cultivate the conditions in which his wife can grow and flourish. This means attending to her particular needs and particular gifts, creating safety and security so that she can take risks, bearing the weight of leadership so that she is freed for her own calling. The gardener's job is not to be the garden's most beautiful plant — it is to tend the garden so that every plant in it flourishes. The husband who asks "What does my wife need to flourish?" and then acts on the answer is a gardener-husband.

verseByVerse.quote: Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The standard is impossible by human effort — and that is the point. No husband can love his wife as Christ loved the church in his own strength. The call to Christlike love drives the husband to his knees, to the cross, to the Spirit — because only the Spirit of the crucified and risen Christ can produce in a self-centred man the self-giving love that Ephesians requires. The husband who takes this verse seriously will spend the rest of his marriage discovering how far short he falls and how desperate he is for grace. That is not a counsel of despair; it is the doorway to the marriage that God intends — a marriage grounded not in the husband's natural virtue but in the Spirit's supernatural supply.

verseByVerse.quote: Likewise, husbands, live with your wives in an understanding way, showing honor to the woman as the weaker vessel, since they are heirs with you of the grace of life, so that your prayers may not be hindered. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Peter links the quality of the marriage relationship to the effectiveness of the couple's prayer. The husband who dishonours his wife, who fails to understand her, who treats her as less than a full co-heir of grace — his prayers are hindered. This is an astonishing statement: the health of the vertical relationship with God is connected to the health of the horizontal relationship in marriage. The husband cannot compartmentalise — treating his wife with contempt at home and then offering worship with pure hands on Sunday. God notices. The word understanding (kata gnōsin — according to knowledge) calls the husband to genuine attention to who his wife is: her needs, her fears, her gifts, her experiences.

verseByVerse.quote: For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The pattern of leadership in the kingdom of God is servant leadership — and Jesus grounds it not in pragmatics but in his own example. The greatest among you shall be your servant (Matt 23:11) is not merely advice; it is the shape of authority in the kingdom, modelled by the King. The husband who leads by serving — who takes out the rubbish, who gets up with the baby, who sits with his wife in her grief, who bears the weight of the household's needs without making her feel guilty for having needs — is enacting the kingdom's pattern of leadership in his marriage. This is not weakness; it is the power of the cross applied domestically.

verseByVerse.quote: Let your fountain be blessed, and rejoice in the wife of your youth. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Proverbs commands joy in the marriage — not merely duty, not merely faithfulness, but genuine delight in the wife of your youth. The passage (Prov 5:15–19) uses some of the most intimate and joyful language in the Old Testament to describe the husband's delight in his wife. This is significant: the wisdom tradition does not merely call husbands to sacrifice and endurance — it calls them to joy. The husband who has reduced his marriage to duty-performance has not yet arrived at the fullness of what Proverbs envisions. The covenant and the delight are not in tension; the covenant is the container in which genuine delight can safely grow.

4.title: Wives: The Call to Gospel-Shaped Strength
4.overview:
Ephesians 5:22 — "Wives, submit to your own husbands, as to the Lord" — is one of the most misunderstood, misapplied, and therefore feared verses in the New Testament. It has been used to justify abuse, to silence gifted women, and to enforce a patriarchy that the text itself does not endorse. And it has been avoided, dismissed, or explained away by those who rightly recoil from those abuses but who have abandoned the text rather than recovering it.

The context is everything. Ephesians 5:22 cannot be read without verse 21 ("submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ") or verses 25–33 (the husband's call to Christlike sacrifice). The submission called for is not the submission of a slave to a master, or a child to a parent, or a soldier to a general — it is the free, voluntary, intelligent response of a wife to a husband who is himself called to die for her. It is the church's response to Christ — not the response of the weak to the strong but the response of the beloved to the one who gave himself up for her.

The truly remarkable thing about the wife's calling in Ephesians 5 is its dignity. The church's response to Christ is not a diminishment of the church's dignity but the expression of it. The wife who responds to her husband's servant leadership with grace, intelligence, and willing partnership is not less than the husband — she is the living answer to the question that the husband's servant-leadership asks. Together, they are enacting the gospel: the one who leads by sacrifice, and the one who responds with glad, free, beautiful trust.
4.theology:
The meaning of submission: The Greek word hupotasso (to submit, place oneself under) is used in the New Testament of Christ's submission to the Father (1 Cor 15:28), of Christians' submission to governing authorities (Rom 13:1), and of church members' submission to elders (Heb 13:17). In every case, submission is voluntary, purposeful, and compatible with full dignity and equality of personhood. The wife's submission to her husband is a voluntary act of trust in God's ordering — not a concession of inferiority but an expression of faith. The complementarian tradition (Grudem, Piper, Köstenberger) argues that this order reflects the complementary differentiation within the Trinity: the Son is equal to the Father in nature but submits to the Father in role.

The Proverbs 31 wife: The portrait of the capable wife in Proverbs 31:10–31 is striking in its scope: she manages a household, runs a business, serves the poor, speaks wisdom, teaches her children, and is praised at the city gates. This is not a picture of passive domesticity — it is a picture of extraordinary competence, energy, and initiative exercised within the sphere of her calling. The biblical portrait of wifely virtue is not smallness but strength deployed with wisdom in the right direction.

Equal heirs, differentiated roles: Galatians 3:28 — "there is neither male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus" — establishes the full equality of men and women before God in Christ. This equality of dignity, worth, and access to grace is not in tension with differentiated roles in marriage — just as the Trinity's full equality of nature is not in tension with the differentiated roles of Father, Son, and Spirit. The egalitarian and complementarian traditions in evangelical Christianity both affirm Galatians 3:28; they disagree about what it implies for role differentiation in marriage and ministry.
4.examples:
The Proverbs 31 wife in practice: The woman of Proverbs 31 has been both over-applied (as a checklist that crushes actual women under impossible expectations) and under-appreciated (dismissed as an ancient domestic ideal with nothing to say to the contemporary working woman). Read carefully, she is a portrait of virtue, not a job description — and her virtue includes financial acumen, generosity, entrepreneurship, and public honour. She is the biblical answer to both the doormat and the superwoman: a woman of strength, wisdom, and character whose life is ordered by fear of the Lord (v.30).

Elisabeth Elliot on surrender: Elisabeth Elliot — whose husband Jim was killed by the Auca people he had gone to reach with the gospel, and who then went to live among his killers — wrote compellingly about submission and surrender not as weakness but as the deepest form of strength. Her books Let Me Be a Woman and The Mark of a Man apply the theology of the cross to gender and marriage: the way up is down, the way to strength is surrender, the way to life is through death. Her life embodied what she taught — and it was a life of extraordinary power and influence.

verseByVerse.quote: Wives, submit to your own husbands, as to the Lord. For the husband is the head of the wife even as Christ is the head of the church, his body, and is himself its Savior. Now as the church submits to Christ, so also wives should submit in everything to their husbands. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The standard is not the cultural norm for wives in Ephesus — it is the church's relationship with Christ. This is both higher and more beautiful than any cultural expectation. The church submits to Christ not because it is forced to but because Christ is worthy, because his leadership is trustworthy, because he gave himself for the church's good. The wife's submission to her husband is patterned on this — a free, intelligent, graceful response to a husband who is himself called to love as Christ loved. The submission that is asked for is not blind obedience but the willing trust that a redeemed person gives to a servant-leader whose authority is held accountable to the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: Strength and dignity are her clothing, and she laughs at the time to come. She opens her mouth with wisdom, and the teaching of kindness is on her tongue. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The woman of Proverbs 31 is clothed not in fashion but in strength and dignity — qualities that make her laugh at the future rather than fear it. Her wisdom is not silent; she teaches. Her kindness is not passive; it is on her tongue, active and intentional. This is the biblical portrait of wifely virtue: strength, not weakness; wisdom, not silence; laughter at the future, not anxiety about it. The source of her fearlessness is the final verse: she fears the LORD (v.30). The woman who has placed her ultimate security in God is free from the anxious grasping that diminishes so many human lives.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not let your adorning be external—the braiding of hair and the putting on of gold jewelry, or the clothing you wear— but let your adorning be the hidden person of the heart with the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which in God's sight is very precious. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Peter is not prohibiting jewellery — he is redirecting the attention from external to internal beauty. The word gentle (praus) is the same word used of Jesus (Matt 11:29) and of those who inherit the earth (Matt 5:5). It is not timidity — it is power under control, strength in service of love. The word quiet (hesuchios) describes a settled, unagitated spirit — not silence but peace. This inner beauty — the hidden person of the heart — is imperishable, unlike physical beauty, and it is in God's sight very precious. The woman who pursues this beauty is pursuing what God himself most values.

verseByVerse.quote: There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The equality of all believers in Christ — across ethnicity, social status, and gender — is the foundation on which all discussion of roles in marriage must rest. The wife who submits is not less than the husband to whom she submits — she is a full co-heir of the grace of life (1 Pet 3:7), equally precious to God, equally redeemed by Christ, equally indwelt by the Spirit. The differentiation of roles in marriage does not imply a hierarchy of worth — just as Christ's eternal submission to the Father does not imply that he is less than the Father. Equality of person and differentiation of role are not in tension; they are the pattern of the Trinity, and Christian marriage is called to enact that pattern in the home.

5.title: When Marriage Is Hard: Conflict, Forgiveness, and the Long Road
5.overview:
No Christian couple stands at the altar expecting their marriage to be hard. And yet most marriages, at some point, are. The Romantic myth — that love should feel effortless and that difficulty is a sign that something is fundamentally wrong — is one of the most destructive forces in contemporary marriage. It trains couples to interpret conflict as incompatibility and hardship as evidence that this is the wrong person, rather than as the normal terrain of two sinners learning to live as one.

The Bible is utterly realistic about this. Proverbs is full of the difficulties of marriage: the quarrelsome wife (Prov 21:9, 25:24), the foolish husband (Prov 17:25). The Song of Solomon includes not only rapturous celebration but the experience of separation and the anxiety of love deferred (Song 3:1–4). Paul assumes that married people will have trouble in the flesh (1 Cor 7:28) — and names it without apologising for it. The realistic couple does not expect marriage to be a continuous honeymoon; they expect it to be a covenant road that passes through seasons of difficulty as well as seasons of joy.

The gospel is the only sufficient resource for the hard seasons. The couple who can forgive each other — genuinely, repeatedly, without keeping score — is the couple who has understood what God has done for them in Christ. The couple who can speak truth to each other in love, who can receive correction without self-protection, who can serve each other even in the seasons when service is not being reciprocated — this couple is not living by their natural virtue. They are living by the grace that the Spirit supplies. Hard marriages are not failed marriages; they are marriages in which the gospel is being most visibly applied.
5.theology:
The idol of romantic love: Tim Keller identifies the cult of romantic love — what C.S. Lewis called "being in love" — as one of the most powerful idols of the modern West. When romantic feeling becomes the foundation of marriage and its primary justification, then the marriage is only as secure as the feeling — which fluctuates with health, stress, tiredness, and the thousand ordinary pressures of shared life. The couple who has built their marriage on covenant rather than feeling has a foundation that holds when the feeling is cold. And paradoxically, the couple who commits to covenant faithfulness even in the cold seasons often finds that the feelings return — because love is not only a feeling but a practice, and practised love produces felt love.

Forgiveness in marriage: Ephesians 4:32 — "forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you" — is both the model and the motivation for marital forgiveness. The model: God's forgiveness in Christ is complete, costly, and unconditional — it does not depend on the offender earning it or the offended finding it easy. The motivation: the person who has received such forgiveness cannot withhold it from their spouse. The couple who regularly and genuinely forgives — who does not keep accounts, who does not weaponise past failures, who forgives as they have been forgiven — is a couple in whom the gospel is bearing fruit at the most intimate level.

When divorce is permitted: Jesus permits divorce in cases of sexual immorality (Matt 19:9); Paul permits it when an unbelieving spouse abandons the marriage (1 Cor 7:15). The Reformed tradition has also recognised physical abuse as grounds for at least separation, on the grounds that the abusive partner has already broken the covenant by violence. These are permissions, not commands — the redemptive trajectory of the gospel is always toward restoration where that is possible and safe. But the pastor who refuses to acknowledge any legitimate ground for divorce is adding a burden that Scripture itself does not impose.
5.examples:
The couple who stayed: One of the most powerful testimonies to the gospel's power in marriage is the couple who stayed — who endured the hard season, who kept forgiving when forgiveness was costly, who chose the covenant when the feeling argued for exit — and who came out the other side with a marriage deeper, more honest, and more grounded than anything the honeymoon had produced. These couples are not in the magazines. But they are in your congregation, and their story is worth telling — because it is the story of the gospel applied over the long haul.

Gary Thomas on sacred marriage: Gary Thomas's Sacred Marriage asks a provocative question: what if God designed marriage to make us holy more than to make us happy? This is not a counsel of resigned unhappiness — it is the recovery of the biblical vision of sanctification through the closest human relationship. The very things that make marriage hard (living with someone who sees you clearly, who has needs you cannot meet, who sins against you and is sinned against) are the very things that drive you to the gospel. Marriage is not a happiness machine — it is a sanctification machine, and the couple who enters it with that expectation will not be surprised when it is hard.

verseByVerse.quote: Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The three imperatives — kind, tenderhearted, forgiving — describe the emotional and relational texture of a marriage shaped by the gospel. Tenderhearted (eusplanchnos — literally, good-bowelled, a visceral compassion) is the opposite of the hardness of heart that Jesus identified as the root of divorce (Matt 19:8). Forgiving one another as God in Christ forgave you — this is the engine. The couple who regularly returns to the cross, who remembers what they have been forgiven, is the couple who has the fuel for forgiving their partner. Forgiveness that flows from the gospel does not calculate proportionality; it gives freely because it has freely received.

verseByVerse.quote: He said to them, "Because of your hardness of heart Moses allowed you to divorce your wives, but from the beginning it was not so." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus traces divorce to hardness of heart — and immediately, for the honest reader, the hard season of marriage becomes a spiritual diagnostic. The desire to exit the covenant is not merely an emotional response to difficult circumstances; at some level it is the hardness of heart against which Jesus warns. This is not a condemnation of the abandoned or the abused — they are not the ones with the hard heart. It is a warning to the one who finds their spouse inconvenient, who has allowed the heart to calcify toward the person they promised to love. The remedy for hardness of heart is not stronger willpower but the gospel — the Spirit who gives new hearts (Ezek 36:26) to those who ask.

verseByVerse.quote: The beginning of strife is like letting out water, so quit before the quarrel breaks out. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Proverbs is brilliantly practical about marital conflict. The beginning of strife — that first sharpening of tone, that first accusatory word, that first escalation — is like the moment a dam begins to leak. At that moment, the flood is still preventable. Once the quarrel has broken out, the damage accumulates. The wisdom of this verse is the wisdom of early intervention: recognising the moment when a conversation is tipping into conflict and having the discipline to stop it. This requires the kind of self-knowledge and relational attention that only grows with time — and the kind of humility that keeps asking "Is this really worth fighting about?"

verseByVerse.quote: But if you do marry, you have not sinned, and if a betrothed woman marries, she has not sinned. Yet those who marry will have worldly troubles, and I want to spare you that. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's pastoral honesty is refreshing: married people will have trouble in the flesh. He does not say they might, or that bad marriages have trouble — he says those who marry will have trouble. This is not a deterrent to marriage (Paul himself encourages it for those who are not gifted for celibacy) but a preparation for it. The couple who enters marriage expecting it to be uniformly easy will interpret difficulty as evidence of a mistake. The couple who enters expecting trouble — and who has a theological framework for understanding trouble as the terrain of sanctification and the occasion for grace — will interpret difficulty as the normal landscape of covenant love.

6.title: Marriage, Singleness, and the Kingdom
6.overview:
The church has often made the mistake of treating marriage as the normal Christian life and singleness as a problem to be solved. This is a cultural imposition on a New Testament that holds both callings in equal honour — and that, in Paul's carefully argued case in 1 Corinthians 7, actually regards singleness as the higher gift for those who have received it.

Jesus himself never married. Paul never married (or was widowed by the time of his letters). The two greatest figures of the New Testament — the Son of God and the apostle to the Gentiles — lived celibate lives. This should give the church pause before treating the unmarried adult with pity or incomprehension. Singleness in the service of the kingdom is not a deficiency — it is a calling, a gift, and a freedom. The single person is not an incomplete person waiting for marriage to finish them. They are a complete person in Christ, with a particular freedom to devote themselves to the kingdom's work that the married person does not have.

At the same time, marriage is honoured throughout Scripture as a creation gift, a gospel sign, and a profound good. The writer of Hebrews says marriage is to be held in honour among all (Heb 13:4). The single person who longs for marriage is not spiritually immature — they are expressing a legitimate creation desire for the companionship and union that God said was very good. Both callings — marriage and singleness — are honoured by God, both can be lived to his glory, and both point forward to the eschatological reality that surpasses both: the marriage supper of the Lamb (Rev 19:7).
6.theology:
Singleness as gift and calling: Paul uses the word charisma — spiritual gift — for both celibacy and marriage (1 Cor 7:7). Both are gifts of God, neither is superior in every circumstance, and both require the grace of God to live well. The gift of celibacy is not the mere absence of sexual desire — it is the positive capacity to live fully and fruitfully for the kingdom without the specific goods and obligations of marriage. Not everyone has this gift; those who do are freed for an undivided devotion to the Lord that the married person, by definition, cannot have.

The eschatological horizon: Jesus teaches (Matt 22:30) that in the resurrection there will be no marriage — people will be like angels in heaven. This does not diminish marriage in this age (it is a creation gift and a gospel sign for now) but it locates it within the temporal rather than the eternal order. Marriage is not the final reality — it is the sign that points to the final reality: the union of Christ and his church, celebrated at the marriage supper of the Lamb (Rev 19:7–9). The single person who foregoes earthly marriage for the kingdom is living now in the light of that ultimate reality. The married person is enacting a sign of it.

The church as family: The New Testament creates a new primary community that includes both married and single people: the church, the family of God. Jesus explicitly redefines family around allegiance to him (Mark 3:33–35), and the early church operated with a kinship language that made the single person fully embedded in a family — brothers and sisters in Christ, mothers and fathers in the faith. The church that genuinely operates as a family — in which the single person is not isolated and the married couple is not self-sufficient — is a community that embodies the kingdom's redefinition of belonging.
6.examples:
Paul's contentment: Paul writes from prison, in chains, having been beaten, shipwrecked, and rejected — and says he has learned the secret of contentment in all circumstances (Phil 4:11). His singleness was part of his circumstances; it was the context in which he served with undivided devotion. He did not treat it as a tragedy but as a freedom — the freedom that enabled him to be beaten for the gospel without worrying about a wife and children left behind, to travel without a family's schedule constraining his movements, to pour himself out for the churches without dividing his attention. His contentment was not resignation — it was the freedom of one who had found his ultimate satisfaction in Christ.

The wedding at Cana and the marriage supper: Jesus' first miracle was at a wedding (John 2:1–11) — he blessed a marriage celebration, provided the wine of gladness, and revealed his glory in that setting. His final celebration will be a marriage — the marriage supper of the Lamb (Rev 19:7–9). The first and last celebrations of Jesus' earthly ministry and eternal reign are weddings. This is not a coincidence — it is a theological statement: marriage is the sign, and the marriage supper of the Lamb is the reality. Every human wedding is a small rehearsal for the great feast that is coming.

verseByVerse.quote: I wish that all were as I myself am. But each has his own gift from God, one of one kind and one of another. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's wish is pastoral, not prescriptive — he is not commanding celibacy but acknowledging that his own singleness has been a gift that has served the kingdom. The crucial word is charisma: both singleness and marriage are spiritual gifts, distributed by God according to his purposes, neither universally superior. The single person who is tempted to feel that they have the lesser gift should read this verse carefully: Paul — who had more gospel impact than almost any other human being — regards his singleness as a gift that freed him for that impact. The married person who is tempted to feel that the single person is incomplete should read it equally carefully: their completeness is in Christ, not in a spouse.

verseByVerse.quote: For in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Marriage is a temporal institution — glorious, good, and gospel-bearing in this age, but not carried into the next. The resurrection exceeds it: the union with Christ that marriage signs will then be fully present, and no human marriage, however beautiful, can add to that presence. This is not bad news for the married — it is the news that the best is yet to come, that the marriage to which their marriage points is infinitely more satisfying than anything they have experienced. And it is genuinely good news for the single: the thing they have not experienced in this life — the one-flesh union of marriage — is not the best thing. The best thing is what no one has yet experienced fully, and they will receive it in exactly equal measure to every married person who ever lived.

verseByVerse.quote: Let marriage be held in honor among all, and let the marriage bed be undefiled, for God will judge the sexually immoral and adulterous. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The command to honour marriage is addressed to all — including those who are single. The single Christian who honours marriage — who celebrates their married friends' unions, who does not regard the institution with cynicism, who does not use their freedom from its obligations as an occasion for sexual immorality — is fulfilling this command. The warning against defilement of the marriage bed (sexual immorality and adultery) applies equally to the single person (who defiles it by treating sexual union as something other than its covenantal context) and to the married person (who defiles it by adultery or by importing pornographic patterns). Sexual purity is not merely a premarital concern — it is a lifelong calling for every believer.

verseByVerse.quote: Let us rejoice and exult and give him the glory, for the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his Bride has made herself ready. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This is where all the marriages and all the singlenesses are headed: the marriage supper of the Lamb, the consummation of the covenant that all of human history has been moving toward. The Bride — the church, purchased by Christ's blood, washed by his Word, adorned in the righteousness of the saints — is ready. Every human marriage that has pointed to this; every single life that has lived for this; every covenant kept under difficulty and every forgiveness extended at cost — all of it has been preparation for this moment. The best wedding in human history will pale before this one. And everyone who is in Christ will be there.
